topic.title: the third partner
topic.claim: In urban dual-income homes, the house help is the reason the marriage looks equal; her day off shows who really runs the house.

paragraphs: In most urban Indian homes, the marriage has a third partner.
She arrives at 8 and leaves by 11.
Both of you work. Both of you are tired. You split the rent, the EMI, the Netflix.
And the house runs so smoothly that nobody ever has to ask who does what.
Then one morning, the WhatsApp arrives.
"Didi, aaj nahi aaungi."
By 9 AM, the most honest audit of your marriage has begun.
Who does the dishes. Who sweeps. Who remembers the dusting nobody ever noticed she did.
And the audit usually reaches the same finding: the work doesn't split down the middle. It slides back to the wife.
India's own time-use survey says the same: women who do housework spend about five hours a day on it. Men, about an hour and a half.
Here's what nobody says out loud. Urban India never settled who does the housework.
It outsourced the question, for ₹10,000 a month, and called the answer equality.
That money buys back two, maybe three hours a day for the woman of the house.
It's probably the best-returning money the family spends. Nobody budgets it that way.
And the didi who sent that message has a home too.
Her own dishes, her own kids' tiffin, packed at 6 AM before she gets to yours. The equality you paid for ends at her doorstep.
So when that message comes, don't treat it as a crisis. Treat it as a mirror.
One day a month, it shows you who actually runs your house.
She isn't the help.
She's the reason your marriage looks equal.

1a8f8c5ea701b55bfcfa8e2d0a849d6aaf78bd56.broken_premise: None. The statistical premise matches the government's Time Use Survey 2024. In 2024, women aged 6 and above who did unpaid domestic work averaged 289 minutes a day on it, which is close to five hours. Men who did it averaged 88 minutes, about an hour and a half. The 2019 survey gave similar numbers: 299 and 97 minutes. Two small caveats don't change the take. First, these are averages only for people who did any housework, and men take part far less often (27.1% of men against 81.5% of women), so the gap across the whole population is even wider than the post suggests. Second, these are national figures, not figures for urban dual-income couples. The remaining claims are the writer's own reading of everyday life, not checkable facts about a market or law: that a worker comes 8 to 11, that one monthly salary covers much of the housework, and that she is what makes the marriage look equal.
1a8f8c5ea701b55bfcfa8e2d0a849d6aaf78bd56.actual_mechanism: In India, unpaid domestic work is measured by MoSPI's Time Use Survey. For 2024, it found that women who do housework spend about 289 minutes a day on it and men about 88, and that women are about three times as likely to do any at all. In urban homes, a part-time domestic worker paid monthly takes over some of these tasks, such as dishes, sweeping and mopping. When she is absent, the work falls back on the household, and the survey shows that within households it mostly falls on women. That supports the post's point that the paid help hides the unequal split rather than settling it.
